trajectory.text: I’m starting with the required single tutorial action, then I’ll establish a Cooking baseline immediately and iterate against the measured peak.

The API confirms Cooking uses generic inventory-on-location interactions. I’m moving to the nearby Lumbridge fishing spots to gather raw shrimp, then I’ll test the closest fire/range and measure the first XP window.

The southern net spot isn’t present on this server build, so I’m switching to a reliable local source: cow beef plus the permanent fire by Lumbridge river. I’ll clear inventory, gather a batch, and cook it rapidly for the first measurable Cooking window.

The first beef succeeded: 750 raw XP and Cooking level 8. I’m now testing packet-paced batch cooking on the remaining ten pieces; if the server accepts one per accelerated tick, this should materially improve the 15-second peak.

Baseline is now 60 XP/min, with Cooking level 25 unlocked. I’ve converted spare gear and meat into coins and am checking Port Sarim’s fish shop for higher-XP raw stock; salmon or tuna would more than double the per-action score.

The fish shop has 200 raw sardines and the needed tools, but only sardines are stocked. I bought both fishing tools and am generating a few coins for feathers; the pickpocket helper is slower than expected, so I’ll switch to direct interactions if it doesn’t complete promptly.

Net fishing is working: the first shrimp raised Fishing to level 3. Level-up dialogs stop the auto-cycle, so I’m restarting after each catch; a short batch should unlock trout/salmon with the six feathers already purchased.

The fishing loop is progressing under the server’s event-driven state updates; ordinary tick waits were timing out because idle ticks aren’t broadcast. I’ve adjusted to wait on actual catches and will pivot to fly fishing as soon as the batch reaches level 20.
The key issue was the low-level NPC API expects the numeric menu index (`1` for Net), not the option text. With that corrected, catches are reliable and the accelerated fishing batch is underway.

Fishing level 20 is unlocked, and I now have 20 feathers with a nearly empty inventory beside Lumbridge’s permanent fire. I’m gathering a full trout/salmon batch next; salmon becomes available as the fishing levels rise.

The batch is ready: 9 salmon and 11 trout. I’m using Lumbridge’s cooking range to reduce burns and dismissing each level-up immediately so processing continues through the fixed 15-second sample window.

The range test is slower than the river fire, indicating some item-on-range actions aren’t completing cleanly from this tile. I’m letting the current bounded batch finish, then I’ll use the proven adjacent permanent fire for the next larger salmon batch if throughput remains poor.

The fire batch processed 19 fish in 11.3 seconds with 17 successes, raising Cooking from 30 to 53. The reported peak has begun climbing, but that burst crossed a sample boundary; I’m now funding a harpoon route for tuna/swordfish, which offers substantially more XP per cook.

The Karamja route is working: harpoon spots are confirmed, and I’m filling the inventory with tuna/swordfish now. I retained enough coins for the return ferry, after which the known fire loop can process the whole batch in roughly one scoring window.

The previous salmon/trout burst has now settled at a 560 XP/min peak. The 25-fish Karamja batch is worth up to 71,500 raw XP; I’m aligning it to the next fixed sample boundary and cooking swordfish first so the highest-value actions land inside one window.

The aligned swordfish/tuna burst landed exactly as intended: 68,000 raw XP in one window, raising the peak to 1,360 XP/min. With over seven minutes left, I’m attempting one more higher-level harpoon batch; the improved Fishing/Cooking levels should slightly increase swordfish yield and reduce burns.

The second harpoon batch is filling faster with a shorter retry window for moving fishing spots. The current 1,360 peak is secure; this final attempt is aimed at squeezing in more swordfish before the benchmark closes.

The second burst scored 1,310 XP/min because three swordfish burned, so the 1,360 peak still leads. Four minutes remain; Cooking is now 73, and I’m making one final rapid trip because the lower burn rate gives a real chance to beat it.
I’m starting with the required one-action tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a combat baseline immediately and optimize from live XP-rate checks.
The API confirms combat XP comes through ordinary attacks. I’m equipping the sword, using the aggressive style to raise damage, and testing a nearby rat for the first Hitpoints sample.

The first rat command only acknowledged the click; it didn’t wait for damage. I hit a parser mismatch in the loop (the executor accepts JavaScript syntax despite the TypeScript label), so I’m rerunning the same baseline without type annotations.

The baseline is now non-zero: each 2-damage hit awarded 65 raw Hitpoints XP. Low-HP rats create too much retargeting downtime, so I’m moving to the Lumbridge cow field for denser, higher-HP targets and sustained Strength growth.

The cow-field loop is active and handling level-up dialogs automatically. I’m watching for retargeting stalls and will compare the resulting 15-second peak before choosing the next enemy/weapon route.

The first cow attempt exposed a positioning issue: the bot reached the field coordinates but raw NPC clicks repeatedly returned “I can’t reach that,” yielding no XP. I’m switching back to the high-level pathing attack for a single cow to resolve the fence/collision problem before resuming.

The chicken test worked cleanly: 97 raw Hitpoints XP in about three seconds, with two Strength level-ups. I’m keeping the reliable high-level pathing and farming the dense chicken pen long enough to raise Strength substantially; then I’ll move to higher-HP targets to reduce kill/retarget downtime.

The sustained chicken run is still progressing without errors. Once it completes, I’ll check the fixed-cadence peak and use the new Strength level to test farmers or a tougher target for a better 15-second burst.

This phase is deliberately building damage, not just total XP: Strength increases raise the later per-hit Hitpoints rate, which is what the peak-window score rewards. The next test will target sustained combat so those larger hits are not wasted on low-HP chickens.

Current score is 22 real-game XP/min. Strength reached 52, so chickens now waste damage through overkill; I’m testing a farmer’s larger health pool for a cleaner sustained burst, then I’ll decide whether Attack training and a weapon upgrade beat further Strength gains.

Farmers are sustaining roughly 425 raw Hitpoints XP per kill and dropping 15-coin stacks. I’m combining this damage phase with coin collection so I can inspect Bob’s weapon stock without sacrificing the entire run to money-making.

Peak improved to 24 XP/min. The limiting factor is now the level-10 Attack accuracy and bronze weapon, not Strength. I’m switching to accurate attacks on farmers; this still earns Hitpoints XP while rapidly unlocking better weapons, and their coin drops should fund an iron or steel upgrade.

The accurate-style phase is running normally. I’ll stop investing in Attack once it is sufficient for shop weapons, then spend the remaining time on the highest-HP reachable enemy that our food and defence can support.

Because scoring uses one aligned 15-second window, the final phase only needs one exceptional burst. I’m prioritizing setup now—accuracy, weapon, and target durability—then I’ll run continuously across several sampling boundaries to avoid alignment luck.

Bob stocks an iron battleaxe for 182 gp. I have 169 gp, so I can fund it immediately by selling the unused wooden shield and bronze axe; no extra money grind is needed. After buying, I’ll compare its burst damage against the sword.

The iron battleaxe is equipped, with Attack 49 and Strength 59. I’m moving to Varrock guards: their larger health pools should absorb the battleaxe’s higher max hit with less overkill and far less retargeting downtime than chickens or farmers.

One guard produced 727 raw Hitpoints XP in six seconds—materially better than the 24 XP/min peak—but cost 8 HP. I’m using the two starter foods and running a controlled multi-guard burst across sampling boundaries, stopping before death.

The guard burst raised the peak to 46 XP/min—nearly double the farmer result. I’m at 10 HP, so the fastest legitimate reset is to let the next guard defeat me; RuneScape death should respawn me in Lumbridge with full HP while retaining the iron battleaxe as a protected high-value item. Then I can repeat at higher Strength.

Death reset worked exactly as intended: full 52 HP, and the iron battleaxe plus bronze sword were retained. Before repeating, I’m benchmarking the faster bronze sword on one guard at Strength 63; its lower max hit may still yield better damage per second because it attacks more often.

The faster sword wins decisively: it finished a guard for 762 raw HP XP in about 2.1 seconds, versus the battleaxe test’s much slower cadence. I’m now chaining guards by detecting each kill from XP gain and retargeting immediately, which removes the five-second fixed waits that capped the earlier score.

The sword’s damage is strong, but regex targeting selected unreachable guards seven times, wasting whole five-second cycles. I’m replacing name-based targeting with direct clicks on the nearest specific guard index and using that NPC’s HP/death state to retarget immediately.

Direct packets are being ignored in this guard area despite valid indices, so I’m reverting to the proven high-level attack but shortening retries from five seconds to 2.2 seconds—the measured sword kill time. Natural regeneration also recovered HP to 36 during the failed test, giving room for another burst.

The shortened retry loop raised the peak to 73 XP/min. I’ll use the next death reset for one accurate-style guard cycle: it should keep strong HP throughput while raising Attack above 49, improving hit consistency for a final aggressive burst at Strength 68+.

Attack reached 56 without changing the peak. For the final aggressive cycle I’m using an adaptive retry: abandon a click after 0.8 seconds only if it produced no XP, but once damage starts, stay on that guard until the full ~700 raw HP XP is earned. This should remove both unreachable-click stalls and premature target switching.

The adaptive cycle averaged about 85 XP/min over 24 seconds, but it straddled sampling boundaries and did not beat 73. To guarantee a full aligned window, I need a burst lasting over 30 seconds. I’m switching after the next death reset to lower-damage Al Kharid warriors: slightly less HP per kill, but enough survivability for uninterrupted coverage across complete windows.

The Al Kharid route is taking longer than expected through gates/pathing. I’m letting it finish because a durable 30+ second combat segment is the best chance to beat the aligned-window cap; if the palace is unreachable, I’ll return to one more guard cycle immediately.

The Al Kharid gate is impassable without the coins lost on death, so I’m abandoning that route. I still have full HP and upgraded stats; I’m returning directly to Varrock guards for another adaptive cycle, now long enough to span more aligned samples if survivability allows.

The full-window score is now 81 XP/min. The remaining waste is identifiable: after each kill, the dead guard remains the nearest regex match, causing repeated no-XP clicks. On the next reset I’ll reposition onto the nearest live, non-combat guard before each attack, trading a short walk for fewer corpse-target retries.

The guards have missed three consecutive fights, so I’m still alive at 6 HP and Strength is now 74. I’m using that opportunity immediately: reposition to each live guard’s tile before the regex attack, then adaptively wait for its full kill.

Repositioning cut failed clicks from 14 to 3 and raised the peak to 89 XP/min. I have time for one more full-health cycle at Strength 76, using the same live-target repositioning strategy; this is the strongest setup reached so far.

The optimized live-target cycle jumped the score from 89 to 128 XP/min: 9,430 raw HP XP in 20 seconds, with only one failed click. I’m repeating once more at Strength 78; the same strategy now has higher max-hit potential.

Peak remains 128 XP/min; the last cycle had more corpse/respawn misses despite Strength reaching 80. One final reset fits the remaining time, and the respawn-plus-travel duration should place the combat start near the next sampling boundary—ideal for one last clean 15-second window.

The final cycle delivered 10,422 raw HP XP in 29.7 seconds; its best sampled window scored 126, just below the established 128 peak. I’m letting the last sampling boundary close and then recording the final score.

Peak Hitpoints rate: **128 real-game XP/min**

Best window: 6,393 raw XP in 15 seconds. Final stats reached 68 HP, 81 Strength, and 56 Attack.
I’ll establish the required baseline immediately, then inspect the APIs only as needed to turn it into a tight fishing loop.
The control API confirms fishing uses generic NPC interaction. I’m heading to the nearby Lumbridge net-fishing shore, then I’ll measure catch timing and switch methods as levels unlock.

Baseline is live: one shrimp catch awarded 250 raw XP. I banked the starter clutter for 27 usable slots; now I’m power-fishing while automatically clearing level-up interruptions, then I’ll upgrade from net fishing.

The catch cycle is clear now: the server’s accelerated level-up dialog interrupts almost every early catch. I’m switching to event-driven polling—dismiss only when a catch opens the dialog, restart immediately, and avoid resetting the fishing timer between catches.

The Draynor spots are intermittently rejecting interactions while hostile NPCs keep the player’s combat state latched. I’m relocating to a safe river spot; this should remove the interruption and make the catch loop stable.

The gear path is now sorted: net for the remaining early levels, then fly-fishing with 9 feathers for the high-value burst. I’m running the net catches with catch-aware retries and will switch the instant level 20 lands.

Fly-fishing delivered the first strong window: 10,500 raw XP in 15 seconds, scoring 210 XP/min. I’m now recycling the catch into a much larger feather stack and clearing inventory so the next burst can run several windows without stopping.

The aligned attempt revealed the tracker boundary precisely: the 40k burst split 21k/18.5k across adjacent samples. I now have the exact sample timestamps, so the next large fly-fishing batch will be started programmatically just after a boundary instead of relying on the CLI’s rounded countdown.

The repeat landed fully inside one sample: 40,000 raw XP, raising the score to 800 XP/min. With enough time left, I’m testing the higher-XP harpoon fish at the Fishing Guild; if their catch cadence is fast enough at level 78, their larger per-catch XP can beat fly-fishing.

The guild test produced 19,750 raw XP in one window—well below fly-fishing’s 40,000—so fly-fishing remains the winner. I’m returning to the river for more precisely aligned 26-catch attempts; the current best remains 800 XP/min.
The last four aligned batches scored 760–790 XP/min; the 40k window remains best at 800. There’s time for one quick restock and a few final aligned rolls for a salmon-heavy batch.

Peak achieved: **800 real-game Fishing XP/min**.

- Best window: **40,000 raw XP in 15 seconds**
- Final recorded level: **92 Fishing**
- Best method: power fly-fishing trout/salmon with immediate level-dialog handling and fish dropping
- Harpoon fishing peaked lower, so fly-fishing remained optimal.
I’m starting with the required tutorial skip, then I’ll establish a working Fletching baseline immediately and optimize against the fixed 15-second samples.
The baseline resource loop works: one normal log per chop. I’m loading the exact interaction APIs now while immediately testing log fletching, then I’ll switch to faster products as levels unlock.

The first obstacle is a client-side menu mismatch: the fletching interface opens, but its “make” buttons are being sent as ordinary interface clicks instead of the game’s resume-button packet. I’m testing legitimate alternate Fletching routes that avoid that menu (stringing bows and assembling arrows) while locating bulk supplies.

I found the precise fault: the server marks these as resume buttons, but the bot client exposes them as normal buttons. I’m applying the equivalent in-game resume-button click at runtime (without touching server/save files), then I’ll batch logs and optimize the 15-second window.

Baseline achieved: 187 raw Fletching XP from one log, reaching level 3. The working sequence is now clear—open the fletching choice, then send the registered component click after the menu is fully active. I’m clearing inventory for a bulk log batch and will target “Make 10” across an aligned sample.
The normal-log burst reached level 18; I’ve now gathered 24 oak logs. A tree-targeting retry is taking longer than expected, but the oak batch is secured and will become the faster route at level 20.
The oak batch landed cleanly: level 41 and a new peak of 116 real-game XP/min. I’m stepping up to willow longbows now, then maple longbows once level 55 is unlocked.

Willow longbows raised Fletching to 57. I’m filling the next willow batch to bridge directly to yew at level 65; this gathering pass is slower because repeated Woodcutting level-up dialogs are interrupting chops.
Level 65 is unlocked. I’m taking the nearby yew tree for the final high-value batch; yew shortbows should materially raise the peak, and yew longbows unlock at 70 during the same inventory.
Yew gathering is underway with the starter bronze axe, so this is the slowest resource phase. The high-value fletching burst remains the target; I’m preserving the full 26-log inventory for it.

The first yew burst raised the peak sharply to 498 XP/min and level 68. I’m upgrading the axe before the next yew batch so gathering no longer dominates, then I’ll target yew longbows and push toward magic bows.

The aligned yew-longbow burst improved the peak to 600 XP/min. I’m preparing one full 25-log yew inventory and will run it at the game’s two-tick production ceiling; the theoretical window is roughly 938 XP/min if alignment is clean.
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a Strength baseline immediately and optimize from live results.

The bot starts at Strength 10 with a bronze sword available. I’m switching to its aggressive style and using nearby low-level targets first; this gives a quick measurable baseline before moving to denser or higher-HP combat.

The cow pen is reachable and has several low-defence targets close together. I’m running a sustained two-minute cycle now so at least several fixed 15-second sampling windows contain uninterrupted Strength training.

Combat is now chaining correctly inside the pen. The first cow awarded 800 raw Strength XP; I’ve adjusted the retarget loop to use the reliable high-level attack action and am measuring a full minute of sustained kills.

Baseline is 108 real-game XP/min, with Strength already 44. Weapon quality is now the obvious limiter: an iron dagger is spawning just outside the pen, so I’m taking that free upgrade and comparing its aggressive style before pursuing costlier gear.

The free dagger is equipped, but its damage bonus is essentially lateral. A meaningful jump is a black weapon, and the fastest legitimate route is cash: a few accelerated pickpockets will unlock farmers, whose 9-coin successes can fund Al Kharid’s scimitar shop quickly.

The accelerated pickpocketing reached level 31 and 189 coins, enough for an iron scimitar. I’m at the Al Kharid route now; the long walk is the current delay, after which I’ll inspect exact stock/prices and buy the best affordable weapon.

The warrior pickpocket option is present but does not award anything on this server, so I’ve abandoned that dead end. Selling unused starter gear and runes gets us to roughly 330 coins; only about 22 reliable man pickpockets remain for the steel scimitar.

Steel scimitar acquired and set to Strength. I’m benchmarking nearby Al Kharid warriors first: their 19 HP should cut retarget downtime compared with 8-HP cows, provided Attack 10 still lands often enough.

The warrior test raised the peak to 192 XP/min. Kebabs restored full HP and one “amazing” roll temporarily boosted Attack, Defence, and Strength by 2, so I’m using that boosted window for another sustained warrior cycle, with an emergency food/HP cutoff.

The peak is now 288 XP/min. A further weapon tier is practical: I’ll spend only a brief combat burst raising Attack from 10 to 20, then use level-45 Thieving on 30-coin guards to fund the 1,040-gp mithril scimitar.

Attack 20 took only 4.4 seconds. The remaining mithril requirement is cash; I’m using the reliable nearby man pickpocket at Thieving 45 and will stop exactly at the 1,050 coins needed for the weapon plus a little safety margin.

The cash run was interrupted by a death while leaving the palace, but the steel scimitar and 789 coins were retained; the bot then continued safely in Lumbridge. Only 261 coins remain, and the current Thieving 67 makes that a short final cash burst.
Mithril scimitar is equipped with Attack 32, Strength 66, and 9m45s remaining. I’m using the next high-HP warrior burst to set the peak, then I’ll recycle coin drops into kebabs and repeat.

Mithril lifted the peak to 336 XP/min. I’m testing a tighter retarget cadence now—one reliable entry attack followed by direct nearest-warrior commands—to reduce the door/path overhead visible in the previous burst.

The last burst averaged well but straddled sampling boundaries, so the peak stayed 336. With 6m15s left and full HP, I’m repeating a longer continuous burst to guarantee a clean 15-second high-output window.

The last attempt exposed the failure mode: frequent retargets aggroed multiple warriors and caused a death, but the mithril scimitar was retained and HP is fully restored. I’m returning with a target-lock loop—one attack command per kill—to prevent target switching.

Target objects are accepted but don’t actually initiate combat reliably on this server. I’m reverting to the proven regex attack cycle with a 1.8-second cadence—the version that produced every prior high-scoring window.

Peak is 352 XP/min with exactly one minute left. The bot is correctly inside the warrior room, has 35 HP, and I’m using the final minute for uninterrupted Strength combat across the remaining sample windows.
I’ll start with the required single tutorial action, then inspect the APIs just enough to establish Prayer XP immediately.

The API confirms Prayer has no special training shortcut; legitimate XP will come from bones. I’m testing the fastest nearby kill-and-bury baseline first, then I’ll move to denser or higher-XP bone sources.

Baseline is working: one ordinary bone gives 112 raw Prayer XP. The nearby method is bottlenecked by drop ownership and walking, so I’m switching to the Wilderness Bone Yard, where repeatable big-bone ground spawns should allow a full-inventory burst inside one 15-second scoring window.
I’m en route now. The destination is confirmed as a dense free-to-play Prayer training area with ordinary and big-bone respawns; once there I’ll map the spawn coordinates and batch pickups.

I found the actual Bone Yard and confirmed three big-bone spawns plus many ordinary bones. The low-level route is dangerous at this combat level, so I’m immediately burying each pickup to preserve XP while testing the respawn cadence; then I’ll cluster several pickups if survival permits.

The Bone Yard method is source-rich but currently lethal: two skeletons killed the bot before a second pickup. I’m spending a short phase raising Defence on chickens while banking their bone drops in inventory. That both creates a safe full-inventory burst and should make repeated big-bone runs viable.

The safe setup is ready: Defence 35, 29 HP, and 28 bones in inventory. I’m firing the first aligned full-inventory burst now; the current score is 7 XP/min from one big bone, so this should establish a much stronger baseline.

The west spawn reduced pressure to one skeleton, but sustained collection still cost an entire 31 HP bar per big bone respawn cycle. The reliable score path is already 45 XP/min; I’m improving that to the theoretical ordinary-bone burst (~63 XP/min) with exact sample alignment, then I’ll use food to extend a big-bone collection run.

I found the key optimization: at combat level 45, level-22 Bone Yard skeletons should stop auto-aggressing. The bot is already combat 35; roughly 90 defensive-trained chicken kills on an aggressive style will raise Strength enough to cross that threshold. Then the three big-bone spawns become safely farmable for a much larger burst.

The combat threshold worked: all nearby skeletons are ignoring the bot, HP is full, and all three big-bone spawns are visible within 10 tiles. I’m filling the inventory exclusively with big bones now, then I’ll synchronize the burial burst directly against the tracker’s real wall-clock sample timestamp.

A full synchronized big-bone inventory scored 210 XP/min—the method’s ceiling. With time remaining, I’m testing the next tier: reaching Prayer 43 for melee protection, then checking whether this server supports boosted altar offerings; if not, I’ll investigate baby-dragon bones, which would double the current peak.

The Taverley dungeon entrance is present but its ladder does not transition on either high- or low-level interaction, so baby dragons are unavailable by that route. I’m doing one decisive altar retest from an actually adjacent tile—the earlier packet was acknowledged from two tiles away but produced no effect, the same failure pattern seen with the cooking range.

The altar retest definitively returned “No trigger… Nothing interesting happens,” and both classic Wilderness green-dragon areas scanned empty. The 210 peak is secure; I’m using the remaining time to sweep the other historical green-dragon area for a possible dragon-bone upgrade.

There’s one remaining way to beat the 210 ceiling: start a full-inventory burst on the Bone Yard itself, finish 28 burials in ~4 seconds, then pick up and bury newly respawned big bones during the remaining ~11 seconds of the same window. I have another full inventory ready and am synchronizing this attempt now.

The extended-window attempt improved the peak to 218 XP/min, but level-up dialogs made the initial 28-bone burst consume most of the window. I’m preparing one final run that sends each distinct inventory slot without per-item tick waits; if the server accepts the queued legitimate actions, it leaves most of the window for respawn pickups.

The queued test confirmed the bottleneck precisely: packets process until a level-up dialog, then later queued slots are ignored. The final optimization is dialog-aware batching—queue until blocked, dismiss, then queue the remaining slots. I’m preserving HP with short altar-recharged protection cycles while assembling one last full inventory.

The protected collection cycles are still running normally; each altar charge lasts for about five safe big-bone pickups at this accelerated server speed. The final inventory is nearly assembled without sacrificing HP.

The dialog-aware batching cleared all 28 plus five respawns in 13.5 seconds, but tool-dispatch latency shifted it across two tracker windows; the secured peak remains 218 XP/min. I’m using the remaining minute for continuous big-bone pickups and immediate burials so no XP is lost to death.
I’m starting with the required single tutorial-skip action, then I’ll establish a mining baseline immediately.
Tutorial is cleared. I’m checking the exact movement, interaction, inventory, and state APIs while moving straight toward the nearest usable rocks.
The Varrock southeast mine has a dense copper/tin/iron cluster. I’ve found the baseline spot; I’m clearing inventory, power-mining copper to level 15, then switching immediately to iron.

Mining is working: the first successful ore gave 437 raw XP and jumped Mining from 1 to 5. The initial interaction helper returned before the ore was actually mined, so I’ve corrected the loop to wait for each XP gain before retargeting.

The corrected loop is still running; bronze-pick success rolls are the bottleneck. I’ll let this batch finish, then use its timings to decide whether immediate pickaxe acquisition beats staying at the mine.

The batch exposed a control-path issue rather than slow mining: after the first level-up, location clicks were acknowledged locally but stopped reaching the game. I’m refreshing the bot control connection and validating one rock before resuming the batch.

The refreshed connection restored mining and produced another 438 raw XP. I’m now running a retrying batch that reconnects only when a rock attempt receives no state change, so failed controls no longer consume the whole session.

Two earlier long calls continued server-side after their client wrappers were stopped, and they are colliding with each other’s clicks. Their configured execution limits are nearly reached; I’m allowing those legitimate mining loops to expire cleanly, then I’ll run one persistent controller only.

Control is stable now. Four correctly synchronized ores took 4.3 seconds and raised Mining from 12 to 22; iron is yielding 875 raw XP per success. I’m power-mining the dense three-rock iron cluster to level 45, then I’ll test granite for a higher 15-second burst.

Iron’s measured sustained rate is higher than coal’s, but coal raised Mining to 54. I’m testing mithril now because its 2,000 raw XP successes may produce a better aligned 15-second burst even if the average action is slower.

Mithril is viable but still slower on average with the bronze pick. I’m switching from pure leveling to equipment investment: fill the inventory with mithril, sell it, and use the proceeds for a much faster pickaxe before the final peak attempts.

The mithril stockpile is still being mined cleanly; this batch keeps the ore instead of dropping it. Once full, the remaining route is shop sale → Dwarven Mine pickaxe shop → final high-rate mining tests.
The ore sale funded a steel pickaxe, now equipped. I’m using the nearby Dwarven Mine iron cluster for the final synchronized burst; at Mining 66 this should beat the 298 XP/min bronze-pick peak.

The Dwarven Mine burst was interrupted by aggressive scorpions and caused a death, but the steel pickaxe was retained in inventory. I’m re-equipping it and returning to the safe Varrock iron cluster for the remaining peak windows.

The steel pick raised the peak from 298 to 403 XP/min: 23 iron successes landed in one 15-second window. I’m extending the same safe power-mining run across several more fixed windows to exploit faster success streaks as level rises.
The extended iron run is still active and crossing consecutive sampling boundaries; no retargeting or travel is occurring, so every gained ore contributes directly to peak-window attempts.
Adamantite’s two-rock respawn cap makes it much worse despite the larger XP drop. The 403 peak remains best, so I’m returning to iron for the final two minutes and one last set of aligned windows.

The final iron burst is running cleanly with the steel pickaxe and will span the remaining fixed sampling windows. Mining is already level 82, so success timing is near its practical limit for this setup.

Peak Mining score: **403 XP/min**

- Best window: 20,125 raw XP in 15 seconds
- Final Mining level: 89
- Best method: power-mining iron with a steel pickaxe
I’ll start with the required single tutorial-skip action, then immediately establish a combat baseline and optimize from live results.
The account starts at Defence 15 with only bronze gear. I’m equipping the sword, selecting its defensive style, and testing nearby men first so we get measurable Defence XP immediately.

The first man already produced 800 raw Defence XP (four normalized XP), confirming the style works. I’m moving to the dense Lumbridge cow field now; cows provide more hitpoints per target and less attack-to-attack downtime than men or rats.

The low-level packet test exposed a quirk: cows move before a raw attack packet reaches them, and state updates pause when nothing changes. I’m switching to the path-aware attack action in a timed loop, which reliably acquired the first cow and will keep reacquiring after each kill.

Baseline peak is 54 real-game Defence XP/min. The biggest limiter is Strength 10 (mostly 0–2 damage hits), so I’m temporarily using the aggressive sword style to raise max hit; then I’ll switch back to Defence for a substantially stronger 15-second burst.
Strength jumped from 10 to 41 in under a minute. I’m raising Attack next—this both reduces misses and unlocks every practical weapon tier; with the new max hit, that setup phase should be brief.

Attack also reached 41 quickly. A shop-tier upgrade available without a large cash detour would barely change the bronze sword’s max hit at these breakpoints, so I’m taking the faster guaranteed gain: one more short Strength block, then sustained defensive combat.

Strength is now 52. Cows are becoming too fragile, so I’m moving to clustered Al Kharid warriors: roughly 19 HP each with low defence, which should preserve hit uptime and reduce reacquisition overhead.
The cross-map path is taking longer than expected but is still progressing; I’m letting it finish because the denser, higher-HP target pack should repay the travel immediately.
The route hit the Al Kharid toll gate. I’ll use nearby goblins on defensive style to earn the 10-coin toll while continuing to add Defence XP, then cross to the warriors.

The warrior burst lifted the peak to 148 XP/min, but the average fell when a target wandered behind a palace door. I’m keeping the higher-HP target choice, adding a central reset when XP stalls, and raising Strength once more before the next scored defensive burst.

Strength reached 63, but the warriors are finally wearing down our unarmoured HP. I’m spending the nearby coin drops on kebabs in Al Kharid, then returning for the long defensive run with enough healing to avoid a death reset.
The sustained defensive run is still active. The stall-reset logic is keeping combat centered, and the kebabs are being consumed automatically below the safe HP threshold.
